profile.summary: ESM-1b is a protein language model from Meta's FAIR protein team. It reads a single amino-acid sequence and was trained without labels to predict masked amino acids from their context. Its per-residue and per-sequence representations are used as features for structure and function prediction, and its masked-token scores can be used to score the effect of sequence variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: introduction, Model description; paper: abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESM-1b is a 33-layer transformer based on the RoBERTa architecture, with pre-activation layer normalisation. It was trained with the masked language modelling objective: 15% of amino acids are masked and the model predicts them from the rest of the sequence. The training data are raw protein sequences only, with no structure or function labels. The authors found the hyperparameters by a search on 100M-parameter models and scaled them to a model of about 650M parameters trained on UniRef50 representative sequences (UR50/S). The representations can be read out per residue or averaged per sequence, and the attention maps give unsupervised contact predictions.

sections.body: There is one ESM-1b checkpoint, esm1b_t33_650M_UR50S, released with the Rives et al. paper in a December 2020 update. The earlier ESM-1 checkpoints and the later ESM-1v and ESM-2 models are separate models. The model card says ESM-2 will usually perform better and recommends it unless the goal is to compare against ESM-1b. A result should name the checkpoint and, for Hugging Face use, the revision; this page read revision 7b37824b.

steps.title: Load ESM-1b and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import esm

model, alphabet = esm.pretrained.esm1b_t33_650M_UR50S()
batch_converter = alphabet.get_batch_converter()
model.eval()  # disables dropout for deterministic results

data = [
    ("protein1", "MKTVRQERLKSIVRILERSKEPVSGAQLAEELSVSRQVIVQDIAYLRSLGYNIVATPRGYVLAGG"),
]
batch_labels, batch_strs, batch_tokens = batch_converter(data)
batch_lens = (batch_tokens != alphabet.padding_idx).sum(1)

with torch.no_grad():
    results = model(batch_tokens, repr_layers=[33], return_contacts=True)
token_representations = results["representations"][33]

sequence_representations = []
for i, tokens_len in enumerate(batch_lens):
    sequence_representations.append(token_representations[i, 1 : tokens_len - 1].mean(0))
PY
steps.explanation: The README's quick-start example, wrapped in a shell heredoc, with the ESM-2 loader replaced by the ESM-1b loader named in the README's model table, one input sequence kept, and the plotting lines removed. ESM-1b has 33 layers, so layer 33 is the final layer as in the README example.

profile.summary: Protenix is an open-source biomolecular structure predictor from ByteDance, built as a reproduction of AlphaFold3. It takes a JSON description of the molecules in a complex, such as protein chains, ligands and nucleic acids, optionally with multiple sequence alignments and templates, and predicts the all-atom three-dimensional structure of the complex. It is run through a command-line tool that also prepares the alignment and template inputs.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; README: introduction, Quick Prediction; instructions: Inference and CLI Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Protenix follows the AlphaFold3 design: a diffusion model that samples atom coordinates, with recycling over a pairformer trunk and a confidence head. Inference is controlled by the number of recycles and the number of diffusion steps: the base checkpoints use 10 recycles and 200 diffusion steps, while the mini and tiny checkpoints use 4 recycles and 5 steps to run faster. Most checkpoints take multiple sequence alignments; the v1.0.0 checkpoints also take RNA alignments and structural templates, the constraint checkpoint takes pocket and contact restraints, and the ESM and ISM checkpoints add single-sequence protein language model embeddings from ESM2-3B (standard ESM2 embeddings for ESM, ISM embeddings for ISM) and do not use alignments by default.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository lists nine named checkpoints. Their names follow the pattern protenix_{model_size}_{features}_{version}, with sizes base, mini and tiny. The base v1.0.0 checkpoints hold 368.48 M parameters; protenix-v2 holds 464.44 M, mini 135.22 M or 134.06 M, and tiny 109.50 M. Two training data cutoffs exist: 2021-09-30, chosen to match AlphaFold3, and 2025-06-30 for the applied checkpoint. A result must name the checkpoint, because accuracy, cutoff and inference settings all differ between them, and should also name the number of seeds and samples, since the README reports accuracy rising with the sampling budget.

profile.summary: ProGen2 is a suite of autoregressive protein language models released by Salesforce Research, in sizes from 151M to 6.4B parameters. Given a start token or the beginning of a sequence, a model generates amino acids one at a time, so it can write new sequences; the same model also scores an existing sequence by its log-likelihood, which the authors use to predict protein fitness without any fine-tuning. The checkpoints differ in the sequence database they were trained on, which includes genomic, metagenomic and immune repertoire sources.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: title, Models, Setup

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each ProGen2 checkpoint is a decoder-only transformer trained to predict the next token in a protein sequence. The configuration class in the repository sets the shape of a model: vocabulary, context positions, embedding width, number of layers and number of attention heads. Generation is done by the sampling script, which encodes a context string with the model's tokenizer and samples continuations with a temperature and nucleus (top-p) setting. The repository also ships a likelihood script that scores a given sequence. In the README's examples, a sequence is written between the tokens 1 and 2, and free generation starts from the token 1 alone.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Seven checkpoints are published: progen2-small (151M), progen2-medium, progen2-oas and progen2-base (764M each), progen2-large and progen2-BFD90 (2.7B each) and progen2-xlarge (6.4B). They are downloaded as tar.gz archives from a Google Storage bucket; there is no official Hugging Face repository in the sources read, and the archives are not versioned by a revision hash. A result must therefore name the checkpoint, and should also record the sampling settings, because the script's defaults (temperature 0.2, top-p 0.95, max length 256, fp16 on GPU) differ from the values in the README's example command.

The same checkpoint does both jobs: the repository ships a sampling script for generation and a likelihood script for scoring an existing sequence, with no fine-tuning in between.

The scripts assume a CUDA device and fp16 by default, falling back to CPU and fp32; the sources read do not state the GPU memory needed for the 6.4B checkpoint.
The authors ask for care in how generated sequences are used, and for oversight during design and deployment.

profile.summary: Tranception is an autoregressive transformer language model for protein fitness prediction, from the Marks lab and the OATML group. It scores a mutated protein sequence by how likely the model thinks that sequence is, and it can optionally blend that score with counts from an alignment of homologous sequences retrieved at inference time. It handles substitutions, multiple mutants and insertions or deletions, and it was published together with the ProteinGym benchmark.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Tranception is a decoder-only transformer built on two ideas: making attention heads specialise, and reading patterns from contiguous subsequences. The published configuration uses a squared-relu activation, grouped ALiBi position embeddings and a 25-token vocabulary. At inference the model's own autoregressive log-likelihood can be combined with weighted pseudocounts computed at each alignment position, using the sequence weighting procedure of Hopf et al. with the default thresholds. The configuration file carries the retrieval weight for that blend. Scoring insertions and deletions with retrieval also needs Clustal Omega, because the mutated sequence has to be realigned.

A result must say which checkpoint was used and whether retrieval was on (the --inference_time_retrieval flag), and with retrieval it must also name the alignment and the weights file. profile.summary: ProGen3 is a family of generative protein language models released by Profluent. Given a direction marker and an optional partial sequence, a model writes amino acids one at a time, in either the N-to-C or the C-to-N direction, and it can also fill in a span in the middle of a given sequence. The same models score an existing sequence by log-likelihood and perplexity, which is how the repository evaluates them on ProteinGym assays. Six checkpoints are published, from 112M to about 3B parameters, under a non-commercial weights licence.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProGen3 is a sparse mixture-of-experts transformer. The 3B configuration has 24 layers, hidden size 1280, 16 attention heads, 8 experts with 2 chosen per token, SiLU-gated feed-forward blocks, RMS normalisation and rotary position embeddings. It is trained in both reading directions: a prompt starts with 1 for N-to-C or 2 for C-to-N, so the same model can extend a sequence from either end. A separate [GLM] prompt form asks the model to replace a named span of a given sequence with a chosen average number of residues, which is how infilling is done. Scoring averages the log-likelihood of the forward and reverse directions.

profile.summary: ProSST is a protein language model that reads both a protein's amino acid sequence and its 3D structure. The structure is first converted into a sequence of discrete structure tokens, one per residue, and the model is pretrained to predict masked residues. Its main use in the repository is zero-shot prediction of the effect of amino acid substitutions, scored on the ProteinGym benchmark.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProSST has two parts. The structure quantization module serialises a protein structure into residue-level local structures, embeds each one as a dense vector, and assigns it to a cluster of a pretrained clustering model; the cluster index is the residue's structure token. A Transformer then reads the residue tokens and the structure tokens together. Its disentangled attention learns the relationship between the two token sequences explicitly; the config lists attention terms between residues, positions and structure tokens. The model is pretrained with masked language modelling on millions of structures.

The notebook and the ProteinGym command pair ProSST-2048 with structure tokens made at vocabulary size 2048. Because the checkpoints differ in K, a result should name K and the Hugging Face revision. This page read ProSST-2048 at revision e94ffee7. The repository's ProteinGym script also needs precomputed structure tokens; the README links them on Google Drive, made from the same PDB set as ProtSSN.

steps.title: Score mutants on one protein
steps.shell:
cd zero_shot
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer
from prosst.structure.get_sst_seq import SSTPredictor
from Bio import SeqIO
import torch
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import spearmanr

prosst_model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("AI4Protein/ProSST-2048", trust_remote_code=True)
prosst_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("AI4Protein/ProSST-2048", trust_remote_code=True)
predictor = SSTPredictor(structure_vocab_size=2048)

residue_sequence = str(SeqIO.read('example_data/GRB2_HUMAN_Faure_2021.fasta', 'fasta').seq)
structure_sequence = predictor.predict_from_pdb("example_data/GRB2_HUMAN_Faure_2021.pdb")[0]['2048_sst_seq']
structure_sequence_offset = [i + 3 for i in structure_sequence]

tokenized_res = prosst_tokenizer([residue_sequence], return_tensors='pt')
input_ids = tokenized_res['input_ids']
attention_mask = tokenized_res['attention_mask']
structure_input_ids = torch.tensor([1, *structure_sequence_offset, 2], dtype=torch.long).unsqueeze(0)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = prosst_model(
        input_ids=input_ids,
        attention_mask=attention_mask,
        ss_input_ids=structure_input_ids
    )
logits = torch.log_softmax(outputs.logits[:, 1:-1], dim=-1).squeeze()

df = pd.read_csv("example_data/GRB2_HUMAN_Faure_2021.csv")
mutants = df['mutant'].tolist()
vocab = prosst_tokenizer.get_vocab()
pred_scores = []
for mutant in mutants:
    mutant_score = 0
    for sub_mutant in mutant.split(":"):
        wt, idx, mt = sub_mutant[0], int(sub_mutant[1:-1]) - 1, sub_mutant[-1]
        pred = logits[idx, vocab[mt]] - logits[idx, vocab[wt]]
        mutant_score += pred.item()
    pred_scores.append(mutant_score)

print(spearmanr(pred_scores, df['DMS_score']))
PY

profile.summary: RITA is a family of four generative protein language models that read a protein sequence one amino acid at a time, left to right. They were trained on over 280 million sequences from UniRef-100 to predict the next amino acid. They can generate new sequences from a prompt, and the likelihood they assign to a sequence can be used as a zero-shot fitness score for mutants.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each RITA model is a decoder-only transformer trained as a causal language model: given the residues so far, it predicts the next one. The four sizes share this design and differ in width and depth, from 768 dimensions and 12 layers (Small) to 2048 dimensions and 24 layers (XLarge). The paper studies how next amino acid prediction, zero-shot fitness and enzyme function prediction change with model size. For fitness, the repository's script scores each mutated sequence by its log-likelihood under the model, summed over the sequence read forwards and backwards.

profile.summary: ProteinZero V2 designs amino acid sequences for a protein backbone that you supply. It starts from ProteinMPNN and improves it with online reinforcement learning: the model generates sequences, those sequences are folded by ESMFold and scored for structural agreement and predicted stability, and the reward is used to update the model. Two teaser checkpoints are released, for structures of up to about 100 residues.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The base model is ProteinMPNN, loaded with 128-dimensional node and edge features, three encoder and three decoder layers and 48 neighbours per residue. Reinforcement learning then trains it against rewards rather than a single supervised target: the V2 README names structural feedback from ESMFold and the fast change in folding free energy introduced in V1. V1 used GRPO; the V2 checkpoints were trained with PARPO, an algorithm the authors describe as aimed at exploring Pareto frontiers in multi-objective optimisation, and whose formulation is not yet published.

profile.summary: CARP is a family of protein language models built from convolutions rather than attention. Each model reads an amino acid sequence and was pretrained to fill in masked residues, on the March 2020 release of UniRef50. It returns a representation for every residue, plus per-residue logits that can be used to score sequences. Because it is a convolutional network, cost grows linearly with length rather than quadratically.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Convolutional autoencoding representations of proteins (CARP); abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each CARP model is a ByteNet encoder: stacked convolutional layers with growing dilation, so a residue's representation takes in a widening window of neighbours without attention. Pretraining masks residues and asks the model to predict them, as in BERT and ESM-1b. The loader reads the width, depth, kernel size and dilation factor from the checkpoint and builds a ByteNetLM over the protein alphabet, then wraps it so padding is masked. Forward returns per-residue representations; with repr_layers and logits you also get intermediate layers and the vocabulary logits.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four sizes are released and are chosen by name in load_model_and_alphabet: carp_600k, carp_38M, carp_76M and carp_640M. The loader fetches each from one Zenodo deposit, so a result should name the checkpoint and that deposit (record 6564798, dated 2022-03-18). The same loader also serves MIF, MIF-ST and BiGCARP from other deposits; MIF-ST pulls carp_640M in as its sequence model, so a MIF-ST result is not a CARP result.

profile.summary: AlphaFold 2 predicts the three-dimensional structure of a protein from its amino acid sequence. It first searches sequence databases to build a multiple sequence alignment and find structural templates, then runs a neural network that reasons jointly over the alignment and over pairs of residues, and finally outputs atomic coordinates with a per-residue confidence score. This repository is the inference pipeline, and it also includes AlphaFold-Multimer for predicting complexes of several chains.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: AlphaFold; Installation; AlphaFold output; paper, introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The pipeline has two halves. First, standard search tools, which the paper names as jackhmmer and HHBlits, build a multiple sequence alignment from the sequence databases, and templates are taken from homologous structures where available. Then the network runs: a trunk of 48 Evoformer blocks that passes information between the alignment representation and a pairwise representation of residue relationships, followed by a structure module that gives each residue an explicit rotation and translation and so places the atoms. The whole network is applied several times over, feeding its own output back in, which the authors call recycling. A relaxation step with Amber then fixes local geometry, and the five models are ranked by predicted LDDT.
sections.source_locator: paper, Inputs and data sources, AlphaFold network; README: AlphaFold output

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: A result must name three things: the code version, the parameter set and the databases. The presets are monomer, monomer_casp14, monomer_ptm and multimer. The parameter sets are dated tar files, and the README explains how to go back to the 2022-03-02 (v2.2.0) or 2022-01-19 (v2.1.0) multimer weights. The v2.3.0 technical note says the current multimer weights were fine-tuned with a new training cutoff of 2021-09-30, keeping the same model architecture. The databases that the download scripts fetch are not the CASP14 versions, and the README lists the exact CASP14 database releases for anyone reproducing that work. Some targets have high run-to-run variance over random seeds. The authors call AlphaFold-Multimer a work in progress that is not expected to be as stable as the monomer system, and it also needs the UniProt database.

profile.summary: PiFold designs an amino acid sequence for a protein backbone you supply: the inverse of structure prediction. It represents the backbone as a graph of residues, with features built by its own residue featurizer, and predicts all residues in one pass instead of one at a time. The authors report 51.66% sequence recovery on CATH 4.2 with inference about 70 times faster than autoregressive methods.
profile.summary_source_locator: ReadMe.md: Introduction, Framework; arXiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The backbone is turned into a graph: each residue is a node, joined to its 30 nearest neighbours. A residue featurizer builds the node and edge features, including learnable virtual atoms meant to carry information that the real atom positions do not. Ten PiGNN layers then pass messages, mixing node, edge and global context. The decoder emits every residue at once, which is what makes it faster than autoregressive inverse folding models, and training optimises perplexity against the native sequence.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one method and one release. The Training&Data release, published 2023-03-05, carries a trained checkpoint.pth plus the cath4.2 and ts datasets, but the README does not document how to load it, so a PiFold result usually depends on a model someone trained or on the Colab notebooks. The code calls the method ProDesign, its earlier name, and main.py trains from scratch on CATH or TS50 with the defaults in parser.py (batch size 8, learning rate 0.001, up to 100 epochs, seed 111) before testing. A result should say which dataset split, which seed and which checkpoint or notebook it came from.

profile.summary: HyInv does inverse folding: given a protein backbone it proposes amino-acid sequences that should fold into it. The input is the N, C-alpha, C and O backbone atoms of a structure read from a PDB file; the output is a set of sequences, written as FASTA. It is a small graph network of 1,957,573 parameters that was trained first on natural and predicted structures and then by reinforcement learning against a structure predictor, and it ships as an installable Python package with its weights.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraph, Usage, Layout; technical report Sections 2 and 2.1

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: HyInv follows the message-passing encoder and decoder design of ProteinMPNN. Each residue is joined to its 48 nearest neighbours and the edges carry distance features that do not change with rotation or translation. The encoder has 4 layers of width 128 and runs once for a backbone; the decoder has 3 layers of the same width and predicts amino-acid distributions at the masked positions from the backbone and the residues already visible. Training had two stages: supervision that maximised the likelihood of the native sequence under a random residue order, then reinforcement learning whose reward was mostly the scTM between the predicted structure of a candidate sequence and the input backbone. At inference the model needs no protein language model, no structure predictor and no alignment.
sections.source_locator: Technical report Sections 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3; README.md opening paragraph

sections.title: Sampling: draft and rewrite
sections.body: Sequences are not drawn in one pass. The positions are split at random into 8 fixed groups. A draft phase samples one group per round at temperature 0.6 starting from a fully masked sequence, and a rewrite phase then masks one group per round, keeps every other position visible, and resamples that group at temperature 0.34. Generating a design costs one encoder pass and 16 decoder passes. The authors report that separating the two temperatures gives a higher scTM at the same sequence diversity than sampling at a single temperature, by 0.0078 on CATH4.3 test and 0.0131 on RecentPDB, measured on an earlier checkpoint of the same run.
sections.source_locator: Technical report Sections 3.1 and 3.2; README.md opening paragraph

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is released: the reinforcement-learning version, which the technical report identifies as update 640 with draft temperature 0.6 and rewrite temperature 0.34, the setting used for every result in the report. The supervised checkpoint that preceded it is described but not released. A result should name the setting as well as the checkpoint, because the package offers three numerical paths. The default reference path is FP32 and reproduces its own output for the same seed, batch size, device type and PyTorch version; the exact path is accelerated FP32 and almost always returns the same sequences; the bf16 path is a different arithmetic and does not return the same sequences for the same seed. Batch size is part of the seed, because batch k uses seed plus k, and the CPU and GPU random streams differ.

profile.summary: HelixFold3 is the PaddleHelix team's open reimplementation of AlphaFold3. It takes a JSON description of the molecules in a complex, where proteins, DNA and RNA are given as sequences and ligands as a SMILES string or a Chemical Component Dictionary code, builds multiple sequence alignments with the usual search tools, and predicts one all-atom structure of the assembly. The output is a set of mmCIF files with confidence metrics, ranked by those metrics. Code and parameters are published for non-commercial use only.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: HelixFold3 follows AlphaFold3 as described in that paper rather than from released code, and is built in PaddlePaddle on the team's earlier HelixFold, HelixFold-Single, HelixFold-Multimer and HelixDock work. Prediction has two parts. First the pipeline searches genetic databases with jackhmmer, hhblits, hhsearch, nhmmer and hmmsearch to build alignments and finds structural templates up to a template date cutoff. Then the model runs, with a number of recycling passes and a diffusion module that samples several structures for the same input. By default each inference does 5 diffusion samples, and the report's own evaluation used 5 random seeds, 5 diffusion runs per seed and 200 sampling steps, keeping the predictions with the best confidence score.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The first release accompanied a technical report dated August 2024, posted to arXiv on 30 August 2024 and last revised on 23 December 2024. The repository then announced HelixFold3.2 on 23 July 2025, reporting gains on protein tasks in FoldBench and fewer atomic clashes. The parameter file the README links is named HelixFold3-params-20250714.zip, so a result should name the parameter file as well as the repository commit. The README also states the environment it was validated in, Python 3.10, CUDA 12.0, cuDNN 8.4.0, NCCL 2.14.3 and Paddle 3.1.0, and says these settings are needed to reproduce the reported results. Output is not deterministic by default: the number of inference rounds, the diffusion batch size and the random seeds all change the structures produced.

profile.summary: TranceptEVE predicts the effect of mutations in a protein without training on any experimental measurement of that protein. It combines two kinds of model: Tranception, an autoregressive transformer trained across protein families on unaligned sequences, and family-specific models built from a multiple sequence alignment of the protein in question, namely weighted pseudocounts and a trained EVE model. The input is a wild-type sequence, an alignment of its family and a list of variants; the output is one fitness score per variant. The three parts are combined with weights that follow the depth of the alignment, so a protein with a shallow alignment leans on the transformer.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract of PPR582395; score_trancepteve.py argument list; scoring_TranceptEVE_substitutions.sh

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Three sources of evidence are combined at scoring time, not during training. The first is Tranception, an autoregressive transformer with attention heads specialised for contiguous subsequences, which scores a mutated sequence in both directions by default. The second is retrieval from the alignment: weighted pseudocounts at each position, computed with the sequence weighting procedure of Hopf et al. The third is EVE, a family-specific alignment model, whose log probabilities are estimated by sampling and averaged over several trained seeds. The scoring script exposes the combination as two coefficients, alpha for the alignment pseudocounts and beta for EVE, and can rescale the alignment and EVE log probabilities to match the temperature of the transformer.
sections.source_locator: score_trancepteve.py argument list; scoring_TranceptEVE_substitutions.sh; Tranception README, Tranception section

sections.title: What a run needs
sections.body: TranceptEVE is not a single downloadable model. A run needs a Tranception checkpoint, an alignment of the protein family, redundancy-based sequence weights for that alignment, and one or more trained EVE models for the same family. The alignments and weights for the ProteinGym proteins are published by the ProteinGym project, 5.2 GB of alignments and 200 MB of weights; the EVE models themselves are not in that list of downloads, and the scoring script takes a path to a folder holding them. The reference settings the maintainers used draw 200,000 samples for each EVE log probability and average five EVE seeds, 0 to 4.

profile.summary: ProtBert is a protein language model with the BERT architecture, trained only on protein sequences with a masked language modelling objective: 15 per cent of the amino acids in a sequence are hidden and the model learns to put them back. It takes an uppercase amino-acid sequence, written with a space between residues, and returns either predictions for the masked positions or a vector per residue, 1024 numbers wide, that can be used as a feature for another model. The developers say it can be used for feature extraction or fine-tuned on a downstream task, and that fine-tuning was more accurate on some tasks.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The architecture is BERT, declared in the config as BertForMaskedLM with 30 hidden layers, a hidden size of 1024, 16 attention heads, an intermediate size of 4096 and a vocabulary of 30 tokens. Unlike the original BERT there is no next-sentence prediction, because each protein sequence is treated as a complete document. Masking follows the original recipe: 15 per cent of amino acids are chosen, 80 per cent of those are replaced by the mask token, 10 per cent by a different random amino acid and 10 per cent left as they are. Sequences are uppercased and split with single spaces, and the rare letters U, Z, O and B are mapped to X. Training ran on one TPU Pod V3-512 for 400,000 steps, 300,000 at sequence length 512 with batch size 15k and 100,000 at length 2048 with batch size 2.5k, with the Lamb optimiser at learning rate 0.002.

profile.summary: Ankh is a family of protein language models with an encoder and a decoder, in the shape of a T5 model. You give it an amino-acid sequence and the encoder returns a vector per residue that can be used as a feature for another model, for example to predict secondary structure, localisation or solubility. The authors' stated aim was not scale but protein-specific optimisation: they ran over twenty experiments on masking, architecture and pretraining data to get the same or better results with fewer parameters than the larger models of the time. The later Ankh3 models add a second pretraining task, completing a sequence from its first half, so they can also generate the rest of a sequence.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The published configuration of Ankh Base is a T5 encoder and decoder: 48 encoder layers and 24 decoder layers at model width 768, 12 attention heads, a feed-forward width of 3072, gated GELU activations and a vocabulary of 144 tokens. Word embeddings are not tied between encoder and decoder. For feature extraction the encoder is used on its own. Pretraining corrupts the sequence with sentinel tokens and asks the decoder to name the missing residues. Ankh3 adds a second task: the first half of the sequence goes to the encoder and the decoder generates the second half. Because Ankh3 was trained on both tasks, its inputs carry a prefix, NLU for representation extraction and S2S for sequence completion.

profile.summary: EVE (evolutionary model of variant effect) predicts whether a single amino acid change in a human protein is likely to cause disease, without training on clinical labels. For each protein it learns from a multiple sequence alignment of that protein's family across organisms. The output is a score per missense variant giving the probability that it falls in the pathogenic cluster, with an uncertainty on that assignment.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README: Overview, Data requirements

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: EVE has three steps. First, a Bayesian variational autoencoder (VAE) is trained on a re-weighted multiple sequence alignment for one protein family and learns a distribution over its sequences. Second, the trained VAE gives each single amino acid mutation an evolutionary index, which approximates the log-likelihood ratio of the mutant against the wild type. Third, a global-local mixture of Gaussian mixture models splits the variants into a benign and a pathogenic cluster on that index, and the EVE score is the probabilistic assignment to the pathogenic cluster. In the default settings the encoder has hidden layers of 2000, 1000 and 300 units, the latent space has 50 dimensions, and the decoder is Bayesian.
sections.source_locator: README: Overview, Usage; EVE/default_model_params.json

sections.title: Alignments and precomputed scores
sections.body: The developers built each alignment with five Jackhmmer iterations against UniRef100 (downloaded on 20 April 2020), using EVcouplings, and chose a bit score threshold per protein to balance coverage and depth. This gave training data for 3,219 clinically relevant proteins. The paper reports predictions for more than 36 million variants across 3,219 disease genes. Precomputed EVE scores, alignments and ClinVar labels for all proteins are offered on evemodel.org; the repository itself ships alignments and labels for four proteins (P53, PTEN, RASH and SCN5A).
sections.source_locator: README: MSA creation, Usage, Example scripts; paper abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: EVE is a method, not one pretrained network: a separate VAE is trained for each protein, and the repository releases no trained VAE weights. A result should name the code commit, the alignment used (its bit score threshold and preprocessing), the VAE settings file, the number of samples used for the evolutionary index (20000 in the example) and the GMM parameters (the repository ships default GMM parameters). This page read the repository at commit 460d70ef.

profile.summary: ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 (ProtT5-XL-U50, often just ProtT5) is a protein language model from the ProtTrans project. It reads a single amino acid sequence, with no alignment, and produces a 1024-value embedding for each residue, which can be averaged into one embedding per protein. These embeddings are used as features for downstream predictors, or the model is fine-tuned, for tasks such as secondary structure and subcellular localisation.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 is based on the t5-3b encoder-decoder model and was pretrained self-supervised on raw protein sequences. Unlike the original T5, which used span denoising, it was trained with a BART-like masked language modelling objective: 15% of amino acids are masked, 90% of those replaced by a mask token and 10% by a different random amino acid. Sequences are uppercased, rare amino acids U, Z, O and B are mapped to X, and each residue is one token. The configuration has 24 layers, hidden size 1024 and 32 attention heads. For feature extraction the developers recommend the encoder output rather than the decoder.

steps.title: Extract embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5EncoderModel
import torch
import re

device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

# Load the tokenizer
tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained('Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc', do_lower_case=False)

# Load the model
model = T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc").to(device)

# only GPUs support half-precision currently; if you want to run on CPU use full-precision (not recommended, much slower)
if device == torch.device("cpu"):
    model.to(torch.float32)

# prepare your protein sequences as a list
sequence_examples = ["PRTEINO", "SEQWENCE"]

# replace all rare/ambiguous amino acids by X and introduce white-space between all amino acids
sequence_examples = [" ".join(list(re.sub(r"[UZOB]", "X", sequence))) for sequence in sequence_examples]

# tokenize sequences and pad up to the longest sequence in the batch
ids = tokenizer(sequence_examples, add_special_tokens=True, padding="longest")

input_ids = torch.tensor(ids['input_ids']).to(device)
attention_mask = torch.tensor(ids['attention_mask']).to(device)

# generate embeddings
with torch.no_grad():
    embedding_repr = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask)

# extract residue embeddings for the first ([0,:]) sequence in the batch and remove padded & special tokens ([0,:7]) 
emb_0 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[0,:7] # shape (7 x 1024)
# same for the second ([1,:]) sequence but taking into account different sequence lengths ([1,:8])
emb_1 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[1,:8] # shape (8 x 1024)

# if you want to derive a single representation (per-protein embedding) for the whole protein
emb_0_per_protein = emb_0.mean(dim=0) # shape (1024)
PY

sections.body: E1 is a masked language model (the released class is E1ForMaskedLM). In retrieval-augmented mode, homologous sequences are placed before the query, separated by commas, and the model attends across them with block-causal multi-sequence attention, so it can use family-specific evolutionary context without fine-tuning. The configuration has separate position encodings within each sequence and across the whole input, and uses global attention every third layer. The models were trained on four trillion tokens from the Profluent Protein Atlas, in BF16 precision. A `?` character marks a masked position.

profile.summary: Chroma is a generative model that designs proteins: it samples all-atom structures of single chains and complexes, and the matching sequences, by reversing a diffusion process. The user can sample freely or steer the sampling with composable conditioners for symmetry, substructure, shape, fold class or a text caption. It can also redesign the sequence and side chains of a structure given to it.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README: introduction, Sampling, Design, Conditioners

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Chroma uses a diffusion process designed to match the conformational statistics of polymer ensembles: structures are corrupted towards collapsed polymer noise and a network learns to denoise them. The denoiser is a random graph neural network with long-range connectivity, inspired by N-body algorithms, which scales sub-quadratically with the number of residues, plus a layer that solves for a global structure from predicted inter-residue geometries. A second graph-based design network generates sequence and side chains, and conditional random fields are used for the sequence. Conditioners are PyTorch modules that transform the state or add energy, and the total energy is backpropagated so that any composition of them can be sampled with annealed Langevin dynamics.
sections.source_locator: Paper abstract and Fig. 1 caption; README: introduction, Conditioners, Conditioner API

sections.title: Design modes and conditioners
sections.body: The design network is diffusion-aware: it was trained to predict sequence and side chains not only for natural structures at diffusion time t=0 but for noisy structures at all times. The design_t parameter therefore trades exact design (t=0.0) against robust design in a neighbourhood of the target backbone (t=0.5, the repository default), which the developers report improves one-shot refolding. Predefined conditioners cover symmetry, substructure, shape, secondary structure, domain class (Pfam, CATH, taxonomy), text captions and subsequence constraints, and new ones can be written as small PyTorch modules.

profile.summary: DPLM (diffusion protein language model) is a protein language model trained as a discrete diffusion model rather than by masked or autoregressive prediction. It generates protein sequences from scratch or from a partial sequence, and it can also be fine-tuned as a sequence representation model for predictive tasks. Three sizes are released (150M, 650M, 3B), along with a later multimodal family, DPLM-2, that generates structure and sequence together.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: Overview, Key Features, Model Checkpoints; model card

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DPLM is pretrained with a generative self-supervised discrete diffusion objective over amino acid tokens, which the authors describe as generalising language modelling for proteins. Generation is iterative: the user asks for a length and a number of sequences and the model refines tokens over up to a set number of iterations. The released checkpoints use the ESM-2 transformer architecture (the model class is EsmForDPLM, with rotary position embeddings) and each config records the matching ESM-2 model as its base: facebook/esm2_t30_150M_UR50D, facebook/esm2_t33_650M_UR50D and facebook/esm2_t36_3B_UR50D. Beyond free generation, DPLM supports conditioning on a partial sequence (motif scaffolding), on a structure (inverse folding), and steering towards a secondary structure through classifier guidance.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: Key Features, Generation Examples; config.json files

sections.title: The DPLM family
sections.body: The repository holds three families. DPLM (ICML 2024) models sequences. DPLM-2 (ICLR 2025) adds structure tokens and does sequence and structure co-generation, forward folding and inverse folding; it is initialised from a pretrained DPLM checkpoint and trained with LoRA on PDB and SwissProt structures. DPLM-2 Bit, from the 2025 design-space paper, predicts each bit of the quantised structure feature instead of the index. Seven checkpoints are listed: dplm-150m, dplm-650m, dplm-3b, dplm2-150m, dplm2-650m, dplm2-3b and dplm2-bit-650m. This page describes the sequence DPLM models named in the record.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: A result should name the checkpoint (dplm_150m, dplm_650m or dplm_3b), its Hugging Face revision, the code commit, and the sampling settings, above all the number of iterations (max_iter) and the sequence length. The repository changes behaviour over time: in July 2025 the developers changed the default sampling strategy of DPLM-2 to annealing@2.0:0.1. This page read the code at commit 8a2e15e5 and the checkpoints at revisions 49b7125a (150M), 7a7e651b (650M) and 53849d4a (3B).

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Discrete diffusion protein language model, used both to generate sequences and, after fine-tuning, as a sequence representation model.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: ESM-2 style transformer encoder with rotary position embeddings, wrapped as EsmForDPLM: 30 layers and hidden size 640 (150M), 33 layers and 1280 (650M), 36 layers and 2560 (3B).
facts.source_locator: config.json files; model card: checkpoint table

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: For unconditional generation, a length and a number of sequences; the code builds the starting tokens. For conditional use, a partial sequence (motif), a backbone structure (inverse folding) or a secondary structure annotation.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Generated amino acid sequences, decoded from tokens; for DPLM-2 also structures saved as PDB files. Fine-tuned DPLM also gives representations for predictive tasks.

facts.value: 150M, 650M and 3B as the developers label the three checkpoints (30, 33 and 36 layers). No exact count is published in the sources read, and the Hugging Face responses read here carry no parameter count.

facts.value: UniRef50, about 42 million protein sequences, in the preprocessed form published by EvoDiff. DPLM-2 additionally uses PDB structures and AlphaFold2 SwissProt structures.

strengths.text: One pretrained model covers free sequence generation, motif scaffolding, inverse folding and, after fine-tuning, predictive tasks.
Three sizes are released, and the repository's own tables show generation quality and downstream performance rising with size.
strengths.source_locator: README: Protein sequence generation, Representation Learning

strengths.text: The repository publishes the pretraining scripts, the preprocessed UniRef50 dataset and the evaluation scripts, so the training run can be repeated.
strengths.source_locator: README: Key Features, Training, Protein sequence generation

strengths.text: The developers' claim, from the paper abstract and the repository's table: DPLM compares favourably with ESM2 as a representation learner.

limitations.text: The weights carry no stated licence: the Hugging Face repositories declare none, so terms of use for the checkpoints are unclear even though the code is Apache-2.0.
Positions are limited to 1,026 in the configs, so very long proteins do not fit in one pass.
Setup is heavy and GPU-bound: the install script pins torch 2.2.0 built for CUDA 12.1 and builds OpenFold from a vendored copy, and the README examples call .cuda().

Parts of the family are incomplete or still changing: the full implementation of the 2025 design-space paper is not released, representation learning for DPLM-2 and guided generation are listed as to do, and the DPLM-2 default sampling strategy was changed in July 2025.

run_guide.summary: Build the repository environment at a pinned commit and generate five 200-residue sequences with the DPLM 650M checkpoint.
prerequisites: conda, and Python 3.9 as the README's environment command sets.
A CUDA GPU: the install script pins torch 2.2.0 for CUDA 12.1 and the example calls .cuda(). GPU memory for inference is not stated in the sources read.
The repository code is Apache-2.0; the checkpoints state no licence.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone --recursive https://github.com/bytedance/dplm.git
cd dplm
git checkout --detach 8a2e15e53416b4536f03f79ad1f6f6a9cbd5e19d
git submodule update --init --recursive
steps.explanation: The README's clone command with a placeholder URL (https://url/to/this/repo/dplm.git) replaced by the repository address, plus a checkout and a submodule update so the vendored OpenFold matches the pinned commit.

steps.title: Create the environment and install
steps.shell:
env_name=dplm

conda create -n ${env_name} python=3.9 pip
conda activate ${env_name}

bash scripts/install.sh
steps.explanation: The README's environment commands. scripts/install.sh installs torch 2.2.0 for CUDA 12.1, the package itself and the vendored OpenFold.

steps.title: Generate sequences
steps.shell:
model_name=dplm_650m # choose from dplm_150m, dplm_650m, dplm_3b
output_dir=generation-results/${model_name}/uncond_generation

mkdir -p generation-results

python generate_dplm.py --model_name airkingbd/${model_name} \
	--seq_lens 100 200 300 400 500 \
	--saveto ${output_dir}
steps.explanation: The README's unconditional generation command. It downloads the checkpoint and writes generated sequences for each requested length under the output directory.

outputs: Generated sequences written under generation-results/dplm_650m/uncond_generation. The README's evaluation step then computes pLDDT with ESMFold; the sources do not give the exact output file names.
